paragraphs: This formula shows that the act of association involves a mutual undertaking between the public and the individuals. Each individual, making a contract, so to speak, with himself, is bound in a double capacity: as a member of the Sovereign he is bound to individuals, and as a member of the State he is bound to the Sovereign. But the maxim of civil right that no one is bound by undertakings made to himself does not apply here, for there is a great difference between owing an obligation to yourself and owing one to a whole of which you are a part.

We must also point out that public deliberation can bind all the subjects to the Sovereign, because of the two different capacities in which each of them may be regarded. For the opposite reason, it cannot bind the Sovereign to itself. It is therefore against the nature of the body politic for the Sovereign to impose on itself a law that it cannot break. The Sovereign can regard itself in only one capacity, so it is in the position of an individual making a contract with himself. This makes it clear that there neither is nor can be any kind of fundamental law binding on the body of the people — not even the social contract itself. This does not mean that the body politic cannot make undertakings with others, provided the contract is not broken by them; for in relation to what is outside it, it becomes a simple being, an individual.

But the body politic, or the Sovereign, draws its being wholly from the sanctity of the contract. So it can never bind itself, even to an outsider, to do anything that detracts from the original act, such as giving away some part of itself or submitting to another Sovereign. To violate the act by which it exists would be to destroy itself, and what is itself nothing can create nothing.

Once this multitude is united in one body, no one can wrong a single member without attacking the body, and still less can anyone wrong the body without its members feeling it. Duty and interest therefore bind both contracting parties equally to help each other, and the same men should seek to gather into their double capacity all the advantages that go with it.

Again, the Sovereign is formed wholly of the individuals who compose it, so it has no interest contrary to theirs, and it cannot have one. Consequently the sovereign power need give its subjects no guarantee, because it is impossible for the body to wish to hurt all its members. We shall also see later that it cannot hurt any one of them in particular. The Sovereign, simply by being what it is, is always what it should be.

This is not the case, however, with the relation of the subjects to the Sovereign. Despite the common interest, the Sovereign would have no security that the subjects would fulfill their undertakings unless it found a means of making sure of their loyalty.

In fact, each individual, as a man, may have a particular will that is contrary or unlike the general will which he has as a citizen. His particular interest may speak to him quite differently from the common interest. His absolute and naturally independent existence may make him see what he owes to the common cause as a free gift, the loss of which will do less harm to others than paying it is burdensome to himself. And, regarding the moral person that makes up the State as a persona ficta, because it is not a man, he may wish to enjoy the rights of a citizen without being ready to fulfill the duties of a subject. If such an injustice continued, it would be bound to ruin the body politic.

So that the social compact may not be an empty formula, it tacitly includes an undertaking that alone can give force to the rest: whoever refuses to obey the general will shall be compelled to do so by the whole body. This means nothing less than that he will be forced to be free. For this is the condition that, by giving each citizen to his country, protects him against all personal dependence. In this lies the key to the working of the political machine. This alone makes civil undertakings legitimate; without it they would be absurd, tyrannical and open to the most frightful abuses.
